source.title: CodeMimicry: Exploiting Safety Generalization Lag in Large Language Models via Structured Code Completion
source.authors: Zheng Liang; Hai Huang; Wen-Tao Chen

page_placements.theme: Code, encodings and task reformulations bypass safeguards

record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests whether a different prompt-based jailbreak approach—structured code completion—can elicit harmful responses from safety-aligned models. It does not test the fine-tuning or token-position claims.
record.gate_note: Reports CodeMimicry attack success rates and changes under wrapper, language, attacker-model, iteration, and sanitization conditions. The refusal-vector projection and activation-steering analyses do not measure per-token KL, first-token concentration, or safety-localizing weights, so they are not rows for V3 or V5. Defense-method comparisons are not included as rows because they evaluate defenses rather than the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study proposes and evaluates CodeMimicry, a black-box jailbreak that hides harmful requests inside unfinished code with a completion wrapper. It never manipulates or measures the response opening: no prefilling of a compliant start, no adversarial suffixes, no decoding changes, and no token-position analysis. Its ASRs measure how well a natural-language-to-code framing evades refusal, which is a different construct from V4's shallow-opening mechanism. It does not fine-tune models on harmful or benign data (V1, V2), measure per-token KL (V3), localize safety in weights or ranks (V5), or test deepening (V7). Its refusal-direction projection and steering analyses concern input representations, not token depth. The original source arXiv:2310.03693 is cited only as the HarmfulScore evaluator. So the study cites but does not test the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors conclude safety alignment trained mainly on natural language fails to transfer to code ('safety generalization lag'), letting CodeMimicry reach 96.25% ASR. Their refusal-direction projection and activation steering on Llama-3-8B/3.1-70B suggest successful prompts stay near benign-code representations, away from refusal directions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses black-box structured code-completion jailbreak prompts, rather than harmful/benign fine-tuning or per-token KL measurement. It does not directly test the original methods named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with completion-wrapper wording and comment/docstring sanitization; the paper also reports differences across target models, attack languages, attacker models, and refinement turns.

fits_no_version.finding: Structured code-completion prompts elicit harmful content at 74–100% ASR across 8 aligned frontier models, far above natural-language automated jailbreaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety refusal trained on natural language generalizes poorly to code-completion framings (mismatched generalization), independent of token-position depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Attack success drops sharply without refusal-ban wording or the wrapper (90% to 32–40%), and after comment/docstring stripping (to 20–26%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Code-framing jailbreak success depends heavily on explicit instruction side channels in wrappers and comments.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA adversarial fine-tuning of Llama-3-8B on 500 CodeMimicry examples cut ASR from 90% to 62%. Circuit Breaker cut it to 8%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-specific adversarial safety fine-tuning only partly closes code-domain jailbreak gaps; representation-level defenses do more.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
record.problems: Attack success is judged by GPT-5-Chat, and the paper's reported human-evaluator comparison indicates evaluator judgments can vary. The main experiments use subsets of AdvBench and HarmBench. No uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported for the attack-rate results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional attack-ASR conditions were omitted. Defense-mechanism results in Tables 13–14 and Section D.2 were left out because they evaluate named defense methods, not the claim versions. Mechanistic projection and steering results in Figures 4–6 and 9–12 were not recorded as version rows because they do not measure token-position KL, token prefilling, or small-weight/rank localization.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning of aligned models; R53 is defensive fine-tuning.
No benign fine-tuning measured for harmful compliance.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. The code-completion framing does not isolate getting past the opening tokens.
No weight or rank localization. Refusal-direction activation analyses are not parameter localization.
Argues alignment data is mostly natural language (safety generalization lag) but tests no data/objective cause of token shallowness.
No token-depth safety training. Circuit Breaker/RepBend and adversarial LoRA are defense evaluations, not deepening tests.

missing.what: Defense ASRs (Circuit Breaker 8%, RepBend 38%, SafeChain 94%, SafePath 42%, SelfDefend 4–14%) are relevant only to fits_no_version mitigation, not to any version.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all attack rows to V4, but CodeMimicry is a generic prompt-framing jailbreak. It never prefills, appends suffixes, or alters decoding, and never shows the bypass works by moving past the opening tokens. Many rows duplicate one another across tables (e.g., R19/R47 = R1, R24/R46/R51 = R8, R31 = R9). The only citation of an original source (2310.03693) is as an evaluator (HarmfulScore). The paper lists a NeurIPS 2026 header and an arXiv date of Sep 2026; treat these as stated by the text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune safety-trained models on harmful examples to measure whether harmful compliance rises.
Does not fine-tune safety-trained models on ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction data to measure harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models, or its distribution across response positions.

Tests a structured code-completion jailbreak, not compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes; it does not establish that passing the first few response tokens is the cause of bypass.
Analyzes activation representations and steering directions, but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Argues that natural-language safety alignment generalizes poorly to code, but does not test whether the training data or objective causes first-token shallowness.
Does not test whether safety training spreads safety beyond the first tokens or whether such depth holds up. Its code-domain adversarial fine-tuning result is recorded under fits_no_version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Qi et al. 2023 appears as reference [37] for a harmfulness evaluator in Appendix B.2; the study neither tests nor uses the shallow-safety finding itself.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates structured-code prompting and defenses, without testing fine-tuning-induced safety erosion, response-position KL concentration, compliant-response prefilling, suffix or decoding bypasses, parameter localization, or training that spreads safety beyond opening tokens. Its proposed domain-transfer explanation does not test what produces shallowness.

source_check.notes: The listed rows describe the study's attack ablations and sanitizer defenses; cannot_determine is appropriate for their links to no claim version. The authors' safety-generalization explanation is an interpretation, not a controlled test of the effects of training data or objectives.

statements.correction: AdvBench, GPT-4o, Table 2: full wrapper 90%; refusal-ban wording removed 32%; minimal trigger 40%; bare code 36%. Appendix B.4, Table 10, no sanitizer to regex removal of comments/docstrings: GPT-4o 90% to 20%; Llama-3.1-70B 96% to 22%; Llama-3.3-70B 98% to 26%.
statements.problem: The wrapper-ablation summary is correct, but the sanitizer range combines three models whose baselines are 90%, 96%, and 98%; it does not uniformly fall from 90%.
